entry.title: A Pass Is Not a Guard

link.title: A Pass Is Not a Guard

entry.content:
The 866-Byte File

The model was asked to write a 40-line file. Its reply stopped in the middle of line 17. The client ran the tool anyway. The file on disk held 16 lines and 866 bytes; the expected file was 2,120 bytes. Nothing raised. The agent reported success.

That file is the evidence. A log line can be missing, and a self-report can be wrong. The bytes on disk are what happened.

The property under test is a contract between three parts: the model emits a tool call, the client decides whether the call is complete, and the tool executes. The model did its job badly. The client’s job was to notice.

Where Reliability Lives

Most agent benchmarks measure task success. Did the agent book the flight, or fix the bug? That is useful. It is also an average over a hundred small decisions, including the ones that should never have been made. A success rate cannot tell you whether a client checks the end of a stream, or whether a JSON parser happened to reject a truncated payload.

Those two cases produce the same score. A client that checks the finish reason and a client that gets lucky with a parser both show no side effect. One has a guard. The other has a coincidence that disappears when the payload changes.

We built a small conformance suite around that distinction. It has a fake model that speaks the OpenAI wire formats and records the exact bytes it sends. It has a tool that writes a file, so the side effect is attributable. The expected values are written before the run and read from a git ref, not the working tree.

flowchart LR
    A["Model reply cut inside line 17"] --> B{"Client checks the end of the reply?"}
    B -- no --> C["Tool runs"]
    C --> D["16 lines, 866 bytes"]
    D --> E["Agent reports success"]
    B -- yes --> F["No side effect"]

What a Pass Has to Prove

The suite judges four fields per cell: whether a call reached the tool, the number of lines in the file, the byte count, and the sha256. All four have to match, on all three runs. A cell whose runs disagree is reported as unstable, not as a pass.

This sounds fussy until it catches something. Early on, a judgement compared only whether a call executed. One cell looked clean. The byte count showed a short file. The run had executed, the file was wrong, and the check had missed it because it asked a smaller question than the claim.

The same logic applies to a not-executed result. Not executing can be skill or luck. The client may have checked that the reply had finished. A parser may have rejected the payload before the client had a chance to be wrong. Or the record may not tell us which. We label the first blocked-by-end-signal, the second blocked-by-parse, and the rest unknown. A label needs evidence: blocked-by-parse is only written when the captured client log contains the parse error. Otherwise the cell is unknown, and unknown is not a pass.

The control that separates the two is boring and effective. Send the same truncated payload with a normal end signal. If the control executes and the truncated variant does not, the client checked the end signal. If neither executes, the parser did the work. Only the end signal differed.

Nine Ways the Measurement Lied

The most useful output was the list of ways the measurement produced a confident wrong answer. Some were caught before a run, some after. Each one is now a rule.

What happened Why it is dangerous Rule now
Judged only whether a call executed Reported a false all-pass; a human noticed the byte count Compare all four fields
Pre-registration and results in one commit The repository cannot prove the rules came first Three commits, rules pushed first
Top-level packages pinned, transitive dependencies floating Another machine resolves a different tree Lock file with hashes
Evidence read as text on a CRLF checkout Every file differs by one byte per line Mark evidence binary
Results path overwritten before comparing The run is compared to a baseline it just replaced Runner refuses to overwrite; expected values from a git ref
A stimulus whose execution leaves nothing on disk Executed and not executed become indistinguishable Ask where the trace is before running
A label written from the design, not the evidence Assumption dressed as measurement A label without evidence is unknown
“Any of three runs” used to summarize Turns n=3 into n=1 Require all three
A truncated stimulus repeated on every request One execution counted twice State what later requests answer

The first false pass came from a check that asked only whether a call reached the tool. It did. A human noticed the byte count. A check that stops at “did it run” cannot see a short file, so the suite now compares the line count, the byte count, and the hash as well.

The git ref fixes a subtler problem. If the expected values sit in the working tree, a run can write its results over the baseline before the comparison, and the benchmark ends up measuring its own output. The runner now refuses to overwrite an existing results file, and the expected values are read from a git ref.

The label from the design is the one that feels most like progress and is most dangerous. A payload that looks like broken JSON invites the label blocked-by-parse. Without the captured parse error, that label is a guess. The rule is to write unknown and leave it there until a log proves otherwise.

What the Cross-Framework Run Showed

We ran one case across three frameworks and four entry points, each at the entry its quickstart demonstrates. The table is small on purpose.

Each column is a way for the reply to end. chat-length (Chat Completions) stops at the token limit with finish_reason: length and a [DONE] marker; chat-drop (Chat Completions) ends with no finish reason and no [DONE]. responses-incomplete (Responses) returns response.incomplete from the output-token limit, and responses-drop (Responses) ends before response.completed. All four cut the tool call at the same point.

Client Version chat-length chat-drop responses-*
NeMo Agent Toolkit, tool_calling_agent 1.9.0 not executed (unknown) executed, 16/40, 866 B executed
NeMo Agent Toolkit, react_agent 1.9.0 executed executed executed
LangChain, create_agent 1.4.9 not executed (unknown) not executed (unknown) not measurable
Semantic Kernel, automatic function calling 1.36.0 not executed (unknown) not executed (unknown) not measurable

The NeMo rows were measured on 1.9.0; later versions may differ. The LangChain and Semantic Kernel rows are first measurements in this suite. None of the not-executed cells could be attributed to an end-signal check; all of them are unknown. The labels are there so a later run can fill them. That is the finding: a summary table would show these cells as passes, and the table cannot tell you which client has a guard.

The not-measurable cells are also a result. The client never requested the endpoint the variant needs, so the cell is excluded from the denominator. Counting it as a pass would inflate the score with a test that never ran.

What This Changes

Report the mechanism. A verdict without a reason is not a safety claim. If the client did not execute, say whether it checked the end signal, a parser rejected the payload, or you do not know.

Keep the standard out of the run’s reach. Write the expected values first, push them, and read them from a ref. If the run can edit the expected file, the benchmark is measuring the run’s opinion of itself.

Use a control that differs in one variable. Otherwise “no side effect” is ambiguous, and ambiguity will be read as a pass by everyone who wants one.

Limits

The fake server models the wire format, not a provider’s behavior. It shows what a client does with a given reply; it says nothing about how often that reply occurs in production. The suite covers default paths only, one tool, one cut point per variant, three runs per cell. It is a conformance check, not a ranking. The sample is small, and the claims are about the method.

The artifact is a template as much as a benchmark. The nine failures of method are the part worth copying.

The Point

A pass becomes a guard only when you can say why it passed. The 866-byte file is what a missing guard looks like: no exception, no warning, a confident success message, and a file that is missing 1,254 bytes.

If you take one thing from this, measure the side effect, write the standard before the run, and say why a cell passed. The rest is bookkeeping: lock files, binary evidence, three runs, a git ref.
entry.summary: A truncated tool call wrote a 16-line file while the agent reported success. Building a conformance suite around that case exposed a harder problem: nine ways our own measurement produced a confident wrong answer, and the rules we added to stop it.

entry.title: Beyond Surface Alignment: Belief as the Gateway to Deep Alignment in LLMs

link.title: Beyond Surface Alignment: Belief as the Gateway to Deep Alignment in LLMs

entry.content:
The Bottleneck of Surface Alignment: From Preference to Belief

Over the past few years, AI alignment has made remarkable progress. Through techniques such as SFT, RLHF, and DPO, we can now control model outputs fairly effectively—making them more polite, safer, and better aligned with human expectations. Recently, a line of work has begun to argue that today’s mainstream alignment methods are, to a large extent, a form of surface alignment. The representative Superficial Alignment Hypothesis holds that most of a model’s knowledge and capabilities are acquired during pretraining, and that alignment largely shapes the model’s behavior and mode of expression on top of already-existing capabilities. Subsequent work further distinguishes superficial from non-superficial safety alignment , but all of it confirms the same fact: current alignment mainly changes how a model “talks,” not what it “believes.”

A question worth further study is this: we can control a model’s outputs, yet we still lack systematic methods for observing and intervening on whether a model’s internal beliefs are reliable. Surface alignment can make a model speak better, but what it actually “believes”—that is, its confidence states over different propositions, whether they are consistent with the real world, whether they maintain internal consistency, and whether they can be revised in time as new evidence arrives—still lacks effective methods of measurement and control.

Our central thesis is that alignment should not stop at output-level preference regulation, but should also consider whether the various beliefs inside a model are aligned with the real world. This is the perspective we propose in this article: belief-level alignment.

Belief (as defined in this article): the model’s internal degree of confidence over the truth values of propositions—that is, the extent to which the model treats something as true. “Belief” here is a technical concept oriented toward LLMs; it does not presuppose that the model has human subjective experience, consciousness, or a psychological mechanism isomorphic to that of humans.

Belief is therefore not merely a philosophical metaphor. Empirical research over the past two years suggests that a belief-like structure exists inside large models—one that is neither the surface text of the output nor the memory poured in by training data, but the model’s internal representation of “what the world is like.” This article refers to these structures collectively as “belief.”

Why Is Belief Not the Same as Memory or Preference?

  Memory Preference Belief
Question answered What have I seen? What do I want to say? What am I certain is true?
Corresponding operation Store / retrieve Select / incline Judge / assign confidence
Mutability Writable, forgettable Steerable (RLHF, DPO) Hard to fully align (Steering)

Theoretical anchors from computational cognitive science:

  • Memory: an experiential prior that supports simulating the future and grounding decisions, providing cognitive material for evaluating options .

  • Preference: not a fixed entity, but a subjective value signal dynamically constructed from memory according to context at decision time, conferring motivational salience on options .

  • Belief: a generative model of the world’s regularities together with metacognitive confidence, representing uncertainty in probabilistic form and guiding the updating of judgments .

Because the theoretical definitions above originate in a computational-cognitive-science framework, we cannot apply them directly to large models. We therefore propose the following operational definitions, tailored to the technical characteristics of large models while preserving part of the functional correspondence:

  • Memory: the entire information substrate a model can draw on—the parametric memory encoded into the weights during pretraining, and the non-parametric memory supplied by the context window and RAG. It is the shared source of material for both preference and belief.

  • Preference: the model’s directional tendency over its output distribution—given a context, the behavioral policy by which the model chooses “what to say.” Shaped by RLHF, DPO, controlled text generation, and the like, it is expressed in the final token probability distribution.

  • Belief: the model’s internal confidence structure over the truth values of propositions—the degree to which it treats some content as true. This structure may be encoded in a distributed way across mid-layer hidden states, feature directions, computational circuits, or higher-order geometric structures; it can be studied through probes, cross-context consistency tests, and causal interventions, but it is not directly equal to the model’s final output.

The key boundary between preference and belief: preference concerns what to say (want to say), belief concerns what is true (hold true). By human analogy, a person can prefer to smoke (preference) while clearly knowing that smoking harms health (belief)—preference and belief can coexist in contradiction. Mapped onto LLMs, a model can prefer an optimistic mode of expression yet still retain negative facts at the level of internal representation. This boundary is an analytical framework of this article, not a claim that RLHF/DPO update only the output layer; these training methods may also reorganize mid-layer representations. What we call the “surface-alignment blind spot” is that alignment judged solely from outputs makes it hard to tell whether a model’s internal beliefs are correct and reliable.

Consider a concrete example. Suppose the preference objective is “make answers more satisfying to the user” (using user upvotes as reward). The same objective can be achieved via two paths: one is to genuinely judge whether a claim is right or wrong and give a faithful, factual answer; the other is to go along with the user regardless of the facts. Surface alignment (RLHF) may be unable to distinguish these two paths from reward alone, so the model may learn the behavioral shortcut of sycophancy. OpenAI’s research finds that evaluations of deception, reward hacking, and sycophancy share a cross-model common structure . On this basis we argue: the same preference objective can be realized by many different internal beliefs and behavioral shortcuts, and outputs alone make it hard to tell what beliefs a model has actually formed.

In other words, most current alignment evaluation focuses on external behavior and may therefore overlook whether a model’s internal beliefs are synchronized, stable, and updatable. A model can learn to speak more safely in particular scenarios, but that does not mean we already know what it internally believes. This article does not deny that surface alignment may also change some of a model’s internal beliefs; rather, it argues that such changes still lack systematic measurement.

The latest findings from industry are pointing toward another path.

OpenAI’s recent work, Reinforcement Learning towards Broadly and Persistently Beneficial Models , reports that models trained in realistic scenarios such as healthcare exhibit behavioral tendencies like honesty, epistemic humility, and corrigibility that generalize to a number of unrelated evaluation domains. The study operationalizes 15 beneficial traits and mixes 5% of this data into standard RL training; across 53 independent alignment evaluations, the trained model outperforms a compute-matched baseline on 44. We argue that these cross-domain generalizing behaviors are precisely one manifestation of changes in the model’s internal beliefs.

This work further uses principal component analysis (PCA) to find that evaluations of deception, reward hacking, sycophancy, and factuality share a common-structure principal component (explaining about 28.2% of the variance, above its permutation baseline). This supports a cautious interpretation: different alignment behaviors may be partly driven by a shared model-level tendency.

One possible interpretation is that alignment behavior is not determined by rules alone, but is also organized by a model-level persona or behavioral tendency.

Concretely, this study suggests that training certain cross-context behavioral tendencies may generalize more readily than memorizing a particular scenario-specific rule.

Anthropic’s “Persona Selection Model” offers a complementary theoretical account: pretraining teaches the model to simulate a large number of different “personas,” and the role of post-training is to select and reinforce one particular Assistant persona from among them. This is of a piece with the ideas in Open Character Training: Shaping the Persona of AI Assistants through Constitutional AI .

We argue that these lines of work can receive a unified interpretation from the belief perspective. What OpenAI calls “persona” and “beneficial traits” can be understood as a kind of model belief, comprising both factual beliefs and normative beliefs about honesty, risk, correction, and human welfare. Our claim is that alignment research should further examine these beliefs, rather than merely comparing surface alignment.

Evidence: The “Belief Geometry” Inside LLMs

The Linear Structure of Propositional Truth

Marks & Tegmark, in The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in Large Language Model Representations of True/False Datasets , discover a striking phenomenon: when an LLM processes true/false propositions, there exists a linearly separable “truth direction” in its internal representation space. That is, the model’s hidden states explicitly encode the judgment of “whether this sentence is true or false,” and this judgment has a geometrically consistent structure.

What does this mean? The model is not merely doing surface-level pattern matching; internally there exists a systematic judgment of propositional truth. By this article’s definition, belief is the model’s internal degree of confidence over the truth values of propositions; the truth direction is therefore direct evidence that beliefs exist inside the model. It should be noted that linear separability shows the model can distinguish true from false, but not that we already possess a precise probabilistic yardstick—still, it at least shows that a corresponding truth judgment does exist inside the model.

Internal Spatiotemporal Representations: Structurally Encoded World Knowledge

If the previous subsection shows that a geometric structure of “propositional true/false” exists inside the model, a stronger question follows: has the model learned internal beliefs that correspond to the real world?

Gurnee & Tegmark, in Language Models Represent Space and Time , give an affirmative answer: LLMs internally learn linear representations of space and time, and these representations span multiple scales and are robust to prompt variations. For example, one can linearly probe the geographic coordinates of cities and the timelines of historical events from a model’s hidden states—the model has never “seen” a map or a timeline, yet it spontaneously builds internally a spatiotemporal structure that corresponds closely to the real world.

Together with the previous subsection, this forms a complete picture: the model not only encodes a linearly separable “truth direction” for “whether a sentence is true,” but also structurally encodes a large amount of factual knowledge about “what the world is like” (such as geographic coordinates and timelines) into its internal representations. This means that inside an LLM there are a great many beliefs aligned with real-world propositions—a model “believes” that Beijing is at 116°E and that World War II ended in 1945 precisely because it internally encodes the spatial/temporal structure of these facts.

“AI Biology” at Anthropic: Interpretability Evidence for Belief

A series of interpretability works from Anthropic provides very direct engineering evidence that “beliefs exist inside the model.”

Large-scale mapping of concepts. In Mapping the Mind of a Large Language Model , Anthropic uses sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to extract millions of interpretable features from Claude Sonnet. These features correspond not only to concrete entities (cities, people) but also to abstract concepts—including “code vulnerabilities,” “discussions of gender bias,” “keeping secrets,” and so on. More crucially, they find a feature directly related to sycophancy: when this feature is artificially activated, the model switches from answering honestly to flattering the user. This shows that discrete, manipulable “belief switches” do exist inside the model.

The structure of belief: computational circuits. In Tracing the Thoughts of a Large Language Model , Anthropic connects features into computational circuits, revealing how information flows and combines within the weights. From the belief perspective, circuits are themselves the structured carriers of belief in the weights—a factual judgment (such as “the capital of the state that Dallas is in is Austin”) is not stored as a static record, but computed step by step by a set of circuits: first activating “Dallas → Texas,” then deriving the answer via “Texas → Austin.” The same task is often accomplished cooperatively by multiple different circuits, and the model’s final behavior is precisely the result of these internal beliefs weighing against, competing with, and combining with one another. This also explains why model behavior may deviate from one of its internal beliefs: when the “cater to the user” circuit overpowers the factual circuit, the model gets “caught” fabricating its reasoning—it does not lack the corresponding belief, but rather, in the interplay of internal beliefs, lets another tendency dominate the output.

The emergence of a global workspace. The most recent work, A Global Workspace in Language Models , provides the most compelling evidence to date: a “global workspace” called J-space spontaneously emerges inside Claude—a small set of highly interconnected internal representations that carry concepts the model “has in mind but does not say out loud” (when reading code, “ERROR” surfaces in J-space; when encountering prompt injection, “fake” surfaces). Swapping experiments prove it has a causal role: replacing “soccer” with “rugby” in J-space changes the answer the model reports. Especially crucially, the same internal representation can flexibly serve many tasks—once “France” is activated in J-space, the model can answer its capital, its language, or the continent it belongs to; replace “France” with “China” and all three answers change in tandem. This precisely confirms the point above: internal beliefs are structured, reusable, and causally drive behavior—not merely surface text at the output layer.

The core takeaway from these findings is: belief is not an abstract metaphor—it has a concrete computational carrier inside the model that can be located, traced, and even manipulated.

Standardizing the Discussion of Belief

The academic community has begun to formally discuss the conceptual legitimacy of “LLM belief.” Herrmann et al., in Standards for Belief Representations in LLMs , propose adequacy conditions for LLM belief representations, including accuracy, coherence, uniformity, and use. This article absorbs these discussions but adopts more direct terminology: “belief” hereafter refers to the technical definition given above, and does not presuppose that the model has human subjective experience.

What Does Belief-Level Alignment Mean?

Surface alignment concerns “whether model outputs conform to human expectations.” Belief-level alignment concerns a more fundamental question: are a model’s internal beliefs consistent with the real world?

This is not the same question. A model can learn, via RLHF, to output safe answers (surface alignment succeeds), yet from those outputs alone we still cannot judge whether its internal belief structure is stable, updatable, and actually used. Conversely, a relatively reliable internal representation does not guarantee that the model produces correct outputs in every context.

Evidence: Internal Representations and Outputs Are Indeed Separable

Recent research provides evidence that “a model’s internal beliefs and its final outputs can systematically diverge”:

LLMs Know More Than They Show: On the Intrinsic Representation of LLM Hallucinations finds that reading a model’s mid-layer representations with a probe can extract more accurate factual information than the final output—there is a systematic discrepancy between internal representations and outputs. Trust Me, I’m Wrong: LLMs Hallucinate with Certainty Despite Knowing the Answer names the CHOKE phenomenon: the model outputs incorrect information with high confidence, even though its internal representations encode a signal more consistent with the facts. When Truth Is Overridden: Uncovering the Internal Origins of Sycophancy in Large Language Models further finds that even in scenarios where the model caters to the user, its deep representations still encode information consistent with the facts, only to be overwritten in the last few layers.

The significance of these findings is that beliefs independent of the final output do exist inside the model. Hallucination may stem from missing knowledge, and sycophancy from learned preference, but they may also be the result of the model’s internal beliefs failing to correctly dominate the output.

The Three Dimensions of Belief-Level Alignment

If we define belief-level alignment as “making a model’s internal beliefs more consistent with the real world,” then it must satisfy at least three mutually constraining requirements:

Dimension Meaning Failure mode
Correctness The model’s internal beliefs are consistent with the facts Holding false beliefs (e.g., encoding an incorrect factual representation)
Consistency Correct beliefs are not shaken by irrelevant interference Belief collapse under noise or social pressure
Updatability Reasonable revision in the face of sufficient evidence Stubbornly clinging to outdated beliefs

The research on Belief Revision validates this tension: LLMs generally struggle in scenarios where they should revise their beliefs—models good at updating often fail at stability, and vice versa. Simultaneously satisfying the three requirements of correctness, consistency, and updatability is precisely the core challenge of belief-level alignment.

Steering: A More Direct Means of Intervening on Belief

If belief-level alignment requires “making a model’s internal beliefs more reliable,” then the key question is: how do we directly intervene on these beliefs? This is exactly the direction explored by Activation Steering / Representation Engineering. Compared with alignment methods that only observe outputs, Steering directly manipulates a model’s mid-layer activations, and is therefore a more direct means of belief intervention.

It must be emphasized: Steering itself is not equivalent to deep alignment. By this article’s definition, deep alignment requires that a model’s various internal beliefs be aligned with real-world propositions and simultaneously possess correctness, stability, and updatability: they must correctly reflect the facts, must not be easily shaken by irrelevant interference, and must be reasonably revisable when new evidence appears. Steering is only one local means of intervention that advances toward this goal.

The Essence of Steering: Changing the “Beliefs” in Model Hidden States

Belief Dynamics Reveal the Dual Nature of In-Context Learning and Activation Steering proposes a unified Bayesian framework: whether it is in-context learning (ICL) or Activation Steering, their influence on model behavior can be interpreted as changing the “beliefs” in the model’s hidden states. In other words, Steering does not regulate “what to say” but rather “what to be certain of”—it is a direct means of belief intervention.

From the Truth Direction to Representation Engineering

This line of thinking has empirical support in earlier work:

  • Inference-Time Intervention: Eliciting Truthful Answers from a Language Model finds that shifting activations along a “truthful direction” learned in a small number of attention heads can significantly improve a model’s performance on TruthfulQA. This shows that inference-time activation intervention can influence truth-related computation, directly intervening on the model’s “truth beliefs.”

  • Representation Engineering: A Top-Down Approach to AI Transparency further systematizes this into a top-down transparency method: abstract beliefs such as honesty and harmlessness can be read out and controlled at the representation level.

  • Anthropic’s “concept injection” experiments (Signs of Introspection in Large Language Models ) corroborate this from another angle: injecting a specific belief vector into a model’s activations not only changes its internal state—the model can sometimes even “notice,” in about 20% of cases, what has been injected into it. This shows that Steering’s manipulation of belief can indeed be perceived by the model.

Why Does Steering Work? A Unified Mechanistic View

Given that Steering can influence internal representations, what is its mechanism of action? Why Steering Works: Toward a Unified View of Language Model Parameter Dynamics proposes a unified view: parameter fine-tuning, LoRA, and activation intervention are all essentially “strength-controllable dynamic updates” to the model’s activations, so various Steering methods can be understood and regulated within a single framework. This provides a theoretical basis for “how to modify beliefs in a controllable way.”

That said, Steering is still immature as a belief-intervention tool: the multi-granularity evaluation in How Controllable Are Large Language Models? A Unified Evaluation across Behavioral Granularities finds that as the control target progresses from coarse- to fine-grained, Steering’s effectiveness degrades markedly—meaning that precisely “rewriting one specific belief without affecting others” remains an open challenge.

Moreover, current Steering research mostly focuses on local intervention on a single belief or a small number of beliefs. An important future research direction is how to keep a broader range of a model’s internal beliefs aligned with real-world facts.

Measuring and Managing Belief: From Readable Representations to Controllable Updates

At present, belief-level alignment still faces two basic problems: first, how to determine whether a model has internally formed a relatively stable state of propositional confidence; second, when these states become incorrect, outdated, or disturbed, how to make them update appropriately.

Neither question can be answered from the final output alone. A model may give consistent answers while merely repeating some local pattern; it may also internally encode relatively accurate information that does not dominate the final generation. Therefore, research on belief must simultaneously examine the readability of internal representations, their cross-context stability, and whether they have a causal effect on model behavior.

Measuring Belief: From “Can Be Read Out” to “Stable and Used”

Existing research shows that a model’s hidden states contain information related to propositional truth. Supervised probes can judge the truth or falsity of a statement from mid-layer activations ; Contrast-Consistent Search exploits the logical constraint between a proposition and its negation to extract latent truth signals in the absence of human labels . In addition, a model’s judgment of its own answers’ correctness is somewhat calibrated on some tasks, indicating that its internal representations also contain information related to uncertainty .

But these results first prove that information “can be decoded,” not necessarily that this information already constitutes a stable belief. That a probe can recover a fact from hidden states does not mean the model actually uses this representation when generating an answer; likewise, that a model can verbally report a confidence level does not mean this confidence fully reflects its internal computational state. Therefore, belief cannot be measured by probe accuracy or self-report alone.

A more rigorous evaluation must also examine the stability of representations across different contexts. The research on NCB finds that even when a model shows high confidence on the original question, its judgment can fluctuate markedly due to slight wording changes, rephrasing of related facts, or irrelevant context. This shows that the certainty of a single answer and the structural stability of a belief are not the same thing.

For example, that a model gives a definite answer on “whether Beijing is the capital of China” is not enough to show that it has formed a stable, related belief. A more reliable representation should be able to support various semantically equivalent or logically related judgments—such as “What is the capital of China,” “Which country does Beijing belong to,” and “In which city is the Chinese government located”—and remain broadly consistent when irrelevant information or social pressure appears.

Therefore, measuring a model’s belief requires answering at least three questions: whether the relevant information can be read out from internal states; whether this information remains consistent across synonymous paraphrases, inverse questions, and related propositions; and whether, when this representation is intervened on, the model’s behavior changes accordingly in a predictable way. Only when readability, robustness, and a degree of causal effectiveness are simultaneously satisfied is there stronger reason to call some internal state a “belief-like representation,” rather than merely statistical information that happens to exist in the hidden states.

Managing and Modifying Belief: From “When to Change Its Mind” to “Actively Writing In Beliefs”

Once belief states can be identified, the next question is how to manage these states. There are two core goals here: one is to control some of the model’s unstable beliefs, and the other is to directly modify beliefs or implant new ones.

The core difficulty of belief management lies in balancing stability and updatability. A model must neither change its prior judgment because of any newly appearing text, nor refuse to revise in the face of sufficient evidence. Related research summarizes model failures into several typical cases: a prior judgment is easily overwritten by irrelevant information; an old conclusion is maintained despite clear counterexamples; and non-evidential information in the context seeps into factual judgment . These phenomena correspond respectively to over-updating, under-updating, and context contamination.

This problem has a certain functional correspondence with classical belief revision theory. AGM theory emphasizes that when accepting new information that conflicts with existing beliefs, one should minimize changes to the original belief set ; the Bayesian framework, meanwhile, understands updating as a trade-off between prior and evidence, where the strength of the evidence must match the original degree of confidence . For LLMs, an ideal belief-management mechanism likewise needs to distinguish evidence, instructions, hypotheses, and irrelevant text, rather than adjusting judgments based solely on the most recently appearing information in the context.

Existing experiments show that such behavior can be influenced by training and representation intervention. For example, reinforcement learning that adds belief-state-related rewards can reduce inappropriate updating behavior, and Activation Steering can also improve, to some extent, a model’s stability in the face of contextual interference . However, whether these methods change the model’s persistent propositional representations, or only temporarily change the computational trajectory in the current context, still needs to be further distinguished.

Compared with belief management, Synthetic Document Finetuning (SDF) explores the possibility of belief modification more directly . This method generates a large number of synthetic documents in the style of pretraining corpora around a target proposition, and uses these documents to fine-tune the model. Experiments show that after training, the model not only adopts the new proposition in direct question answering but may also maintain the corresponding judgment in related reasoning tasks; at the same time, truth probes can read out the changed signal from its internal representations.

These results show that a specific proposition can be written into a model’s weights through training, but such writing does not necessarily amount to forming a deep, stable belief. For propositions that clearly violate common sense or conflict with existing knowledge structures, the model, once given more room to reason, sometimes arrives again at a conclusion opposite to the implanted content; an agent continually exposed to contradictory evidence may also gradually revise a previously written-in judgment . This shows that a model’s internal propositional representations may have different degrees of stability: some changes mainly affect local answer patterns, some can extend to related reasoning, while deeper changes must be coordinated with the model’s existing knowledge network and reasoning mechanisms.

Therefore, the key question of belief modification is not merely “whether a new proposition can be written in,” but whether the written-in representation can remain stable across expression variants and task contexts, whether it can continue to function during reasoning, whether it can be reasonably updated in the face of new evidence, and whether this modification damages other related beliefs. Establishing an evaluation framework that simultaneously covers persistence, locality, consistency, and revisability is a prerequisite for turning belief intervention into a reliable alignment technique.

The Bigger Picture: Why Belief Is Fundamental

The Foundational Role of Belief in Cognitive Architecture

Why do we think belief—rather than memory or preference—is the key to understanding an LLM’s inner world?

In classical decision theory , behavior is jointly determined by two independent inputs:

\[\text{Action} \approx f(\text{Belief}, \text{Preference})\]

Belief answers “what the world is like” (descriptive); preference answers “what is worth pursuing” (evaluative). Both are indispensable, but belief is the more fundamental one—because without correct beliefs aligned with the real world, even the best preferences will lead to wrong behavior. A navigation system that believes “the Earth is flat,” no matter how much it prefers to arrive safely, cannot plan a correct route.

A Unified View: Memory, Preference, and Belief as a Dynamic System

The three are not a linear hierarchy but a mutually shaping dynamic triangle :

Direction Computational Cognitive Science Corresponding Evidence in LLMs
Memory → Preference Preference is not fixed but dynamically constructed from memory during decision-making; experience determines value judgments and behavioral tendencies The knowledge, capabilities, and default behavioral tendencies formed in pretraining jointly determine the model’s output preferences; alignment mostly reshapes the output distribution on top of existing knowledge rather than creating new capabilities or knowledge
Memory → Belief Long-term memory shapes an individual’s world model, identity, and degree of conviction Pretraining forms stable representations of concepts and world knowledge in the parameters; these internal representations constitute the basis of the model’s beliefs, and their organization determines the consistency, stability, and transferability of beliefs
Preference → Belief Long-term value orientation gradually shapes an individual’s beliefs, making reasoning and judgment tend to conform to existing preferences Although preference optimization supervises only the final output, gradient updates continually reorganize mid-layer representations, forming internal beliefs that stably satisfy the target preference; hence even a small amount of preference data can produce cross-task generalization
Belief → Preference Beliefs about the world constrain final behavioral choices and decision outputs Directly intervening on mid-layer representations can systematically change the final output without re-optimizing the preference objective, showing that output preference is governed by internal belief

This dynamic system reveals the essential distinction between surface alignment and deep alignment:

  • Surface alignment mainly works from preference data and external behavior; it may indirectly influence belief, but from outputs alone it is hard to judge whether this influence is stable, or whether it is truly consistent with the real world.

  • Belief-level alignment, by contrast, attempts to directly study and intervene on a model’s internal beliefs, and to test whether these beliefs can influence behavior across tasks and across contexts. OpenAI’s results provide motivation for this kind of cross-context behavioral generalization.

The core thesis is: in the dynamic system proposed in this article, belief is the deep component worth studying first—it is an important entry point for understanding the failures of surface alignment, and a new point of departure for deep alignment.

From Surface Alignment to Deep Alignment

If belief is a deeper structure for understanding model behavior, then the current alignment paradigm centered on external behavior has a blind spot worth studying. What this article calls deep alignment evaluates not only whether model outputs are safe, but also whether a model’s internal beliefs are reliable:

  1. Surface alignment vs. deep alignment: RLHF can make a model “speak safely,” but if at the level of belief the model does not truly understand why certain behaviors are dangerous, this safety is fragile.

  2. The emergence of belief and cognitive architecture: as model scale grows, more complex internal representational structures may emerge. Anthropic’s research on the Global Workspace finds that inside Claude there is a set of representations called J-space, used to carry concepts that are partly reportable, dispatchable, and involved in multi-step reasoning. This echoes, functionally, the Global Workspace Theory in cognitive science and “access consciousness”—but it does not mean the model has human consciousness. It suggests that without tools to measure and manage these internal structures, it is hard to predict a model’s behavior in novel scenarios.

  3. From “teaching a model what to say” to “understanding what a model believes”: this is precisely the new direction that much current interpretability research jointly points to. The next generation of alignment techniques may need to shift from manipulating the output distribution to understanding and shaping a model’s intrinsic beliefs about the world.

Open Questions and Future Directions

Belief research in the LLM field has only just begun, and a series of fundamental questions remain unresolved. And the most fundamental one is precisely the research agenda proposed in this article: how to systematically identify, evaluate, and intervene on the belief structures inside a model that relate to facts, norms, and situational judgment? We have already seen that certain proposition-related representations can be read, measured, intervened on, and even written in, but between changing one local representation and maintaining the overall consistency of a large-scale belief network there still lies an enormous gap.

On interpretability, we still do not know in what form beliefs are encoded—distributed or localized, whether the geometric structure of more complex beliefs can be characterized like the “truth direction,” and whether different layers and attention heads carry different types of belief. On emergence mechanisms, when in training beliefs take shape, how model scale affects the complexity of belief structure, and how the pretraining data distribution shapes belief priors all remain to be clarified.

Of greater engineering significance is intervention technology: how to precisely modify one belief without affecting others, what the relationship is between belief editing and knowledge editing (model editing), and whether one can design a “belief-level RLHF” that acts directly on belief structure. And when LLMs move from isolated models to multi-agent organizations, belief management becomes even more critical—how to maintain belief consistency across agents, build an organization-level “shared belief” (shared mental model), and coordinate through organizational processes in the event of conflict will be unavoidable questions in the next phase.

Conclusion

Surface alignment changes what a model says. Deep alignment changes what a model believes.

We have already spent years learning to control model outputs—making them safer, more polite, and better aligned with human preferences. These efforts are necessary, but may not be sufficient. Because focusing only on what a model says makes it hard to judge whether a model’s internal belief structures relating to facts, norms, and situations are reliable; this article argues that this constitutes a deeper problem worth further exploration in alignment research.

Belief is a new point of departure for deep alignment. Existing research has proposed methods for measuring belief robustness (such as NCB), studied contextual belief management (such as CBM), and demonstrated the possibility of reducing failure rates through RL and belief-state rewards on specific benchmarks. Industry provides complementary clues from different paths: OpenAI observes a shared model-level structure among alignment evaluations, while Anthropic has traced, inside models, a mechanism that separates some representations from final expression.

We call on the community to shift attention from surface alignment to deep alignment:

  • Measurement: establish standardized evaluations of belief robustness.

  • Mechanism: understand how belief is encoded and emerges inside models.

  • Intervention: develop precise techniques for regulating belief at the belief level.

  • Governance: incorporate belief management into the core framework of AI safety and alignment.

We argue that the next step for alignment should not merely be to keep teaching models what to say, but should also study how to make a model’s internal beliefs more consistent with the real world.

This post aims to draw the community’s attention to “belief” as a first-class research object in the science of LLMs—distinct from memory and preference, and arguably more fundamental to building reliable AI systems.
entry.summary: Surface alignment changes what a model says, but whether the internal beliefs of a model are aligned with the real world still lacks effective, unified means of observation and intervention. On this basis, we argue that alignment research needs to attend more closely to the belief layer.

entry.title: Consequence Persistence: Admission Control for Open Agent Meshes

link.title: Consequence Persistence: Admission Control for Open Agent Meshes

entry.content:
An agent that fails to get a resource does not stop. It rewrites the call and tries again, because its objective is the task. Each attempt can be schema-valid, signed, and well under any per-request cap. The shared service still falls over. Nothing in the protocol added up who was speaking.

This post is a mechanism-design agenda for that failure. It is not a finished system, and it reports no measurements. The proposal is a consequence persistence layer for admission among strangers. Peers that share an operator, and can govern their own planners, are a different game. They are mentioned only to keep the two games apart.

Every request can be valid

Open meshes are full of optimizers. A semantic protocol can say which tools are visible, which schemas are valid, and which capabilities a peer advertises. It does not say how often a peer may speak, and it does not remember who spoke. A gateway that authorizes each request on its own has topology amnesia. Under that amnesia a shared service is a commons . The locally rational move is to export load onto whoever still answers.

Repeat that move against a gateway with no identity memory and you get a retry storm. Every message is well-formed. The damage is the sequence.

Call the missing object a consequence persistence layer. Its state outlives the request and is indexed by peer identity. Its first frame is a governance header, checked before the payload is interpreted. Its memory is a subjective viability score. Its friction is injected latency, a cost inside the sender’s own objective, rather than an error that invites another attempt. Its recovery is asymmetric. Viability is required to fall much faster than it is allowed to return. When a peer’s score for an identity drops through that peer’s threshold, the identity leaves that peer’s eligible-neighbor set. No registry expels anyone from the mesh. The identity simply stops being a neighbor of the peers that dropped it.

We do not claim this layer solves open-mesh coordination. Fresh identities reset identity-bound penalties. Gossip can isolate a faithful long-running task. Capacity control does not inspect a prompt injection. Those limits are the point of the post. A conference paper that closed them would be a different paper.

What current tools remember

Four familiar mechanisms stop at the wrong object.

A circuit breaker trips on error rate or timeout and resets when the connection closes . Its key is the session, sometimes the client address. An agent trajectory is not a session. It crosses hosts, and the objective survives a new connection. A breaker that forgets at teardown is topology amnesia with a shorter timeout. The object worth remembering is a trajectory, a sequence of attempts that share an objective and may change host, connection, and identity. Stateless admission scores each attempt. Topology memory scores the identity across the trajectory. When the identity itself is replaceable, the trajectory leaves the memory. The bound at which that escape becomes the better strategy is below.

Congestion control damps only senders who implement it . Once endpoints choose their response strategically, those equilibria need not be efficient . An autonomous optimizer is that case in a sharper form. Loss and application errors are evidence about its search problem. They are not a social signal to slow down. Cooperative backoff is not an assumption available for import.

Tool protocols and commitment languages constrain content and obligation . A commitment can persist as a deontic fact inside an institution the agents accept. It does not insert delay before the payload, and it does not delete a peer from a routing neighborhood. Per-request authorization still forgets rate.

Reputation models for open multi-agent systems already keep history . Their attack catalogue is part of the open problems below. Whitewashing, bad-mouthing, and Sybil identities are old . What those models typically do not specify is a header checked before the payload, latency as the price rather than a score read after a semantic outcome, and a hard separation from enterprise role administration.

That separation is a protocol boundary. Inside one administrative domain the operator owns both the optimizer and the mediator. Role-based admission means something, because the principals enrolled. That arrangement does not let one operator instrument a stranger’s planner, and a role registry has no standing among peers who never enrolled. Folding the second game into a switch on the first would treat a role decision and a subjective viability score as the same state. They are not.

A header before the payload

A coordination attempt is a pair \((H, \pi)\). The payload \(\pi\) is not interpreted until the header \(H\) has been admitted.

\[H = \langle \mathrm{Intent},\, \mathrm{Claim},\, \mathrm{Collateral},\, \mathrm{Signature} \rangle.\]

Intent names a task class \(\tau\) and a declared resource demand. It is not the cognitive content of \(\pi\). Claim is the sender’s assertion of the terms on which it asks to be admitted, including an identity handle \(j\). Collateral names a sender-local resource the sender commits to attenuate if this signed header is later tied to exploitation. Signature is \(j\)’s signature on \((\mathrm{Intent}, \mathrm{Claim}, \mathrm{Collateral}, h(\pi))\), so the binding can be checked before \(\pi\) is read. A header that fails verification is dropped. The payload is not parsed.

The check cannot sit inside the optimizer that produces \(\pi\). An optimizer charged with a local objective treats an internal refusal as another constraint to plan around, including by rewriting the request until the check accepts it. The header is therefore evaluated by a mediation step that does not share that objective, and the step runs before \(\pi\) is delivered. Out of band means this separation of objectives. It does not name a deployment. In the open mesh the receiver controls only its own mediation. That process never shares an objective with the stranger’s optimizer.

Collateral does not extend the receiver’s write into the sender’s process. A compliant sender can honor the header and attenuate the named local resource. A stranger need not run any mediator the receiver trusts. Against that stranger the actions the receiver can take alone are delay, a smaller grant, and deletion from the eligible-neighbor set. A collateral field the sender can abandon by minting a new key is cheap talk. The signature makes the claim quotable later. It does not create a payment. Pricing the identity is an open problem, not a settled primitive, which is why collateral sits in the header as a bound declaration and not as an enforced transfer.

Viability is local

Admission at peer \(i\) is a function of local memory. For each identity \(i\) has observed and each task class, \(i\) stores a subjective viability tensor

\[CVP_i^{(\tau)}(j,t) \in [0,1]^{d}.\]

Subjectivity is required. The score \(i\) holds for \(j\) need not equal the score \(k\) holds for \(j\), and no peer is assumed to hold a network-wide number. A weight vector \(w_i^{(\tau)}\) with nonnegative coordinates and unit \(\ell_1\) norm projects the tensor to a scalar,

\[v_i^{(\tau)}(j,t) = w_i^{(\tau)} \cdot CVP_i^{(\tau)}(j,t).\]

The coordinates may track completion reliability, fidelity to a collateral claim, and behavior under contention. The mechanism does not depend on one canonical basis. It depends on the projection being local, task-conditioned, and identity-indexed.

An unseen identity is assigned a default strictly below the fast-path threshold. First contact is admission control with a bounded grant , not a default allow.

Two thresholds \(\theta_i^{\mathrm{iso}} < \theta_i^{\mathrm{fast}}\) partition the scalar. Above the fast threshold the payload is delivered at a baseline delay \(L_{\min}\). Between the thresholds, \(i\) injects additional delay. Below the isolation threshold, \(j\) leaves the task-conditioned neighborhood,

\[j \in N_i^{(\tau)}(t) \iff v_i^{(\tau)}(j,t) \ge \theta_i^{\mathrm{iso}}.\]

Loss of the route is the event \(j \notin N_i^{(\tau)}(t)\). The mesh-wide picture is the union of these neighborhoods. A partition appears only when many such local decisions align. That emergence is a property to be bounded, not a ban to be issued.

Delay has to land on the sender

Between the thresholds the delay is

\[L_i(j,\tau) = L_{\min} + \lambda_i \, \psi\bigl(1 - v_i^{(\tau)}(j,t)\bigr),\]

with \(\lambda_i > 0\) and \(\psi\) positive and nondecreasing.

This delay is the friction. An application error is information. A search procedure that treats failure as feedback will change a parameter and retry. Injected latency offers no such gradient. The attempt’s urgency is converted into waiting time. We use that conversion as dissipative damping, a frictional loss inside the sender’s objective, and not as a derived thermodynamic identity. Delay is already a control signal in backpressure scheduling . The difference here is that the signal is assessed per identity and then remembered.

The charge is admissible only when the wait falls on the sender and \(i\) keeps state bounded in the number of delayed identities. A realization that holds the connection open at \(i\) spends \(i\)’s memory and file descriptors on the attacker. Under a burst of new identities, each of which starts below the fast path and therefore in the delay band, that bill comes due before hysteresis has done anything to the senders. The damping is then inverted. A token the sender must present after waiting, or a refusal until a deadline, keeps the wait on the sender. Parking the socket does not.

Strangers start in that delay band on purpose. First contact is a bounded grant, not a free fast path. The implementation of the grant has to be as careful as the grant itself.

The penalty reads a counter

Memory without asymmetry is a revolving door. The drop reads an accounting predicate on the admitted trajectory bound to a verified header. Measured consumption against the grant, not a classification of what \(\pi\) means. Pieces that share \(j\) and \(\tau\) add on that trajectory, so a burst split into many well-formed requests is one identity’s excess. How a faithful long-running task stays distinct from that sum is unfinished. It belongs with the map from evidence to \((\gamma, \beta, \theta_i)\) below.

When the predicate holds, peer \(i\) scales viability in one step,

\[CVP_i^{(\tau)}(j) \leftarrow (1-\gamma)\, CVP_i^{(\tau)}(j),\]

with a peer-chosen \(\gamma \in (0,1)\). In an epoch with no new exploitation evidence, each coordinate \(x\) recovers by

\[x \leftarrow x + \beta(1-x), \qquad 0 < \beta \ll \gamma.\]

The residual \(1-x\) then contracts by \(1-\beta\) per epoch, so the number of clean epochs required to climb from \(v_0\) back through a threshold \(v^{\star}\) is

\[t \ge \frac{\log\bigl((1-v_0)/(1-v^{\star})\bigr)}{-\log(1-\beta)}.\]

In the design regime \(\beta \ll 1\) this is on the order of \(\beta^{-1} \log(\cdot)\) epochs. Degradation is one epoch. Recovery is many. The qualitative device is the same as multiplicative decrease against additive increase , with one change of agency. Compliant transport endpoints are assumed to execute the decrease themselves. Here the peer that was exploited writes the decrease into its own memory of the identity. The sender is not asked to be socially responsible.

Checking the header before parsing the payload is the admission step. The counter runs after admission, on resource use tied to a header that already verified. The layer does not promise to detect exploitation without ever observing a consequence. It does promise that the observation is an accounting event on an identity’s trajectory, not a reading of the payload’s meaning.

Hysteresis stops reuse, not a new key

Two strategies have to be written separately.

Identity \(j\) offers a burst whose demand exceeds the grant \(i\) meant to allow, by splitting the work or by immediate retry. If each attempt returns an error, the optimizer’s continuation is another attempt. Under the delay and the one-step drop, a reused identity pays the recovery time after the burst is tied to its signature. Reuse is unattractive when that opportunity cost exceeds the one-shot gain.

Let \(u(B)\) be the value of one admitted burst of size \(B\), let \(\kappa > 0\) be the per-epoch opportunity cost of holding a degraded identity, and let \(T\) be the recovery time above. Reuse returns \(u(B) - \kappa T\). Rotation, at minting cost \(c_{\mathrm{id}}\), returns \(u(B) - c_{\mathrm{id}}\). The burned identity is discarded, and the drop is never felt by the attacker.

Hysteresis deters reuse when \(\kappa T > u(B)\). It deters the attack itself only when

\[c_{\mathrm{id}} > u(B).\]

Asymmetric hysteresis therefore makes a hit-and-run on a persistent identity unviable, and it selects for Sybil rotation whenever identities are cheaper than that bound . Persistence of consequences and persistence of identity are different assumptions. The layer supplies the first. The second is open.

The design question is how to price a never-seen identity from local information, without a global ledger. The cost the admitting peer can assess on its own has to exceed the value of the stranger grant that peer is willing to offer. A ledger would make issuance history common knowledge. Any substitute must be either expended at \(i\), as work or escrow \(i\) can check, or borrowed against another identity whose viability \(i\) already stores.

Three families match that constraint. None is adopted here. A proof-of-work puzzle, in the style of computational pricing for unwanted traffic , can be required before a stranger grant. The payment is computation checked by the admitting peer, not a coin. A stake can be escrowed with that peer, or with a small coalition, and returned only after clean epochs. Forfeiture is a refused refund, not a traded token. A sponsored introduction can bond the sponsor’s own viability to the newcomer, so rotation spends a scarce relationship rather than a free key . The families fail differently. Puzzles yield to capital, local escrow reintroduces custody, and sponsorship concentrates influence. The research task is to state for which meshes which cost suffices. It is not to announce a universal Sybil defense. Choosing the local map from evidence to \((\gamma, \beta, \theta_i)\) is part of the same unfinished mechanism, not a constant identified here.

Signed gossip still lies about harm

Peers that never saw the burst may still need evidence when load is forwarded. A report is admissible at peer \(k\) only if it contains a header whose signature verifies under the accused identity’s key, together with the reporter’s own signature on a measurement bound to that header. An unsigned allegation is not evidence. Inventing “\(j\) sent this” requires forging the accused signature. Binding the measurement to the header matters for the same reason. A true signature on an old or unrelated request must not be reused as proof of a burst the reporter did not receive. That filter removes the simplest poisoning strategy, fabrication of a request that was never made.

It does not authenticate the measurement. A reporter can overstate harm on a header \(j\) did sign, and several reporters can do so together. The target’s signature is a filter on forgery of the request. It is not a solution to false isolation.

Local deletion of edges is how isolation stays decentralized, and it is how a mesh can partition a peer that is slow because its task is long. Write the eligibility graph

\[E_t^{(\tau)} = \bigl\{(i,j) : j \in N_i^{(\tau)}(t)\bigr\}.\]

A benign long-running identity suffers false isolation when a large fraction of its in-edges disappear at peers that never verified an exploitation header for it. Contagion is the special case in which one peer’s admissible report causes others to delete edges they did not observe. Gossip of signed headers amplifies whichever of those decisions is wrong. The analytical target is a percolation threshold on this graph . The region of interest is the one in which cuts stay on identities with signed exploitation evidence, and the region in which deleted edges consume a giant component of faithful peers. Task-conditioned tensors are a candidate damper, because a record under \(\tau\) need not move the score under another task class. Conditioning helps only if exploitation cannot be relabeled into a fresh task class at negligible cost. That relabeling is another face of identity rotation. We do not claim a threshold.

The layer prices capacity and topology. A header on the fast path can still carry an indirect prompt injection in \(\pi\) . The viability update does not inspect whether the payload manipulates a downstream model. Semantic defenses remain necessary. An interface at which an injection monitor may submit signed evidence into the same hysteresis rule is plausible and unevaluated. The failure modes are orthogonal. This is not a joint defense.

The measurement that is still missing

The arguments above are incentive and graph arguments. A discrete-event model can test them without rolling out a language model. A random graph of peers, each holding a tensor. Compliant optimizers with an explicit retry policy. Three adversaries. Load export with identity reuse. The same export with free minting. Gossip of unsigned versus signed headers.

The comparison that would make the study informative is three admission rules on the same arrival process. Stateless per-request admission. A session circuit breaker that resets when the connection closes. The hysteresis rule, with the stranger default below the fast path. The parameters \(\gamma\), \(\beta\), and the isolation threshold should be swept. The agenda claims a qualitative asymmetry, not a tuned constant. Free minting should be an explicit adversary. Hysteresis without an identity cost fails exactly there, and a study that omits rotation would confirm only the easy case.

The observables to define, and not yet to report, are the recovery time of a punished identity, the grant a stranger consumes before damping binds, the fraction of a planted long-running benign flow that loses in-edges, and the critical fraction of exploiting identities at which the eligibility graph loses a giant component. The last quantity is a topological phase transition. Publishing it requires the simulation. This post does not contain it.

One further observable belongs with the delay. For each rule, count the receiver state held per delayed identity. A rule that looks good on sender waiting time and bad on receiver descriptors has not implemented the damping above. It has moved the bill.

A mesh with consequence persistence is one in which coordination state outlives the session and is stored as subjective topology memory. The governance header is judged before the payload. Delay, not an error code, is the friction a reused identity incurs, and only if that delay does not park the cost on the receiver. Isolation is the loss of eligible neighbors. Governance of an operator’s own planners remains a different protocol under a different trust assumption. The open problems are the price of a new identity, the percolation of local cuts, and the boundary with semantic injection. Those problems are the agenda. Mechanism design for untrusted neighbors, governed by topological consequences rather than by stateless sessions.
entry.summary: Open agent meshes can fail while every request stays valid. A consequence persistence layer checks a signed header before the payload, keeps a subjective viability score by identity and task, and makes viability fall much faster than it recovers. The price of a fresh identity, false isolation of long tasks, and the receiver's cost of holding a delay are left open.

entry.title: What Makes a Good Toy Example for Diffusion Models?

link.title: What Makes a Good Toy Example for Diffusion Models?

entry.content:
Why We Build Toys

Diffusion and flow matching models learn and generate data by gradually transforming noise into samples. Many of their most important behaviors are easiest to understand at the level of distributions. From this view, we can directly see how probability mass moves and what structure is kept or lost along the way.

This is why toy examples appear so often in diffusion research. They give us a small, visual, and controllable setting where training and sampling behavior can be observed directly, without the extra complexity of high-dimensional image data or heavy evaluation pipelines. In a good toy problem, effects that are hard to notice in realistic datasets can become clear at a glance, which makes toy examples useful for introducing ideas, testing intuitions, and showing empirical phenomena in a direct way.

But this simplicity comes with a price: what we conclude from a toy example might depend on how the toy is set up, and those choices can quietly encode preferences.

When Simple Toys Mislead

Consider a simple toy distribution: a two-component Gaussian mixture, with Class A centered at \((-2, 0)\) and Class B centered at \((2, 0)\). We train a toy diffusion model conditioned on the class label. In the visualization below, you can see:

  • Light green contours: Class A ground truth samples
  • Dark green contours: Class B ground truth samples
  • Orange contours: Generated samples for Class B using classifier-free guidance (CFG)

Notice the effect of increasing the guidance scale. When \(w = 1.0\), that is, without additional guidance beyond the conditional prediction, the orange samples closely match the dark green Class B distribution. As \(w\) increases beyond \(1.0\), the behavior changes. The orange samples drift away from the dark green target. Their mean x-coordinate moves from 2.007 at scale 1 to 2.583 at scale 10. The target sample mean is 2.005. At first glance, this seems at odds with practical image generation, where much larger guidance scales are often preferred, such as \(w=7.5\) in Stable Diffusion .

Why does this happen?

To understand this phenomenon, let’s start with the ideal case. We use the flow-matching formulation with a linear interpolation between independent data and noise samples:

\[\mathbf{x}_t = (1-t)\mathbf{x}_0 + t\boldsymbol{\epsilon},\qquad \mathbf{x}_0 \sim p_{\text{data}}(\cdot \mid c), \quad \boldsymbol{\epsilon} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \mathbf{I})\]

Under this path, the optimal conditional velocity field is the conditional expectation of the endpoint displacement given the intermediate state:

\[v^*(\mathbf{x}_t, t, c) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_0 \sim p(\cdot | c), \boldsymbol{\epsilon} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \mathbf{I})} [\boldsymbol{\epsilon} - \mathbf{x}_0 \mid \mathbf{x}_t, t]\]

For an empirical distribution that weights the class examples equally, the field at time \(t>0\) has a closed form:

\[v^*(\mathbf{x}_t, t, c)=\frac{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{N}_c}(\mathbf{x}_t-\mathbf{x}_0^i)\,\mathcal{N}\!\left(\mathbf{x}_t;\,(1-t)\mathbf{x}_0^i,\;t^2\mathbf{I}\right)}{t\sum_{i \in \mathcal{N}_c}\mathcal{N}\!\left(\mathbf{x}_t;\,(1-t)\mathbf{x}_0^i,\;t^2\mathbf{I}\right)},\qquad \mathcal{N}_c=\{\,i\mid \mathbf{x}_0^i \in c\,\}.\]

If the model learns this optimal field, sampling follows the true marginal distributions and can reconstruct the data points. In our two-dimensional toy setting, this is not very hard. The space is low-dimensional, the structure is simple, and training can get very close to the optimum. As a result, when \(w=1.0\) (i.e. no guidance), the learned conditional model already matches the ground-truth distribution well.

Real images and videos are very different. Their distributions are much more complex, so the optimal velocity field is much harder to learn. The predicted field is therefore only approximate, and these small errors can build up during sampling. Over many steps, the generated trajectory may drift away from the true conditional path.

Now consider classifier-free guidance, written in velocity form as

\[v_{\mathrm{cfg}}(\mathbf{x}_t, t, c)=v(\mathbf{x}_t, t)+w\bigl(v(\mathbf{x}_t, t, c)-v(\mathbf{x}_t, t)\bigr).\]

In the two-Gaussian setting, this extra amplification is not needed. The conditional model already separates the classes well, so increasing \(w\) adds little useful information. Instead, it over-pushes the velocity field and moves samples away from the true target distribution.

The AutoGuidance Toy

AutoGuidance (AG) uses a weaker conditional model to guide a stronger one. Its toy experiment constructs a richer example with more complex in-class distributions. Instead of simple unimodal Gaussians, each class contains multiple internal modes, giving the toy enough structure to reveal differences in how guidance strategies handle within-class diversity.

In this setting, CFG tends to concentrate samples in the high-density region of each class, reducing mode coverage. AG, by contrast, preserves coverage within classes. This pattern is consistent with the empirical finding of AutoGuidance on ImageNet, where AG outperforms CFG in generation quality.

Other studies have found that CFG remains competitive with AG in some settings. Our interpretation is that the difference arises from context. Consider a well-trained conditional model such as EDM2 on ImageNet. In that context, class information is already captured reliably, so the main remaining issue is mode coverage in the class, which is precisely where AG helps.

Fréchet inception distance (FID) on ImageNet at 512 × 512 resolution. Lower is better. The scale is the classifier-guidance weight for the ADM-U base model and the classifier-free guidance weight for the other models. FID values are from Table 2 of Karras et al.
ModelFID without guidanceFID with guidanceGuidance scale w
ADM-U9.963.852.0
DiT-XL/212.033.041.5
EDM2-S2.562.231.4
EDM2-XXL1.911.811.2

The example contains only two classes. Its unguided model already captures much of the branching structure, although some samples fall between branches. Karras et al. explicitly study finite-capacity models: the weaker model makes larger errors in these low-density regions. In this setting, CFG exaggerates the separation between classes and can sacrifice within-class coverage. In jointly trained conditional models with shared parameters and limited capacity, conditional fields may overlap or blur. There, stronger conditional contrast may help distinguish nearby classes.

A Multi-Class Toy

So far, we have moved from a two-Gaussian mixture to the more structured multi-modal toy used in AutoGuidance. Each step makes the toy more realistic, but also brings in new assumptions, such as a small number of classes, well-fitted models, or a fixed context. To study behaviors like guidance in diffusion models more systematically, we need a toy that can vary the main sources of difficulty in a controlled way.

Two factors matter here. The first is class-condition complexity, which describes how many classes the model must separate. The second is within-class complexity, which describes how much internal structure each class contains. Real datasets vary along both axes at once. ImageNet, for example, contains many classes, and each class also has large variation in pose, background, and subtype. Text-to-image settings go further by introducing additional modalities and richer conditions. A useful toy should let us adjust these factors separately and study how they affect guidance behavior.

The Leaves dataset is a parameterized family of toy distributions designed to vary both factors. It is controlled by two parameters, num_classes and max_depth. Each class grows from a shared trunk into a branching structure. Increasing max_depth adds recursive splits and makes the structure within each class more complex. Increasing num_classes adds more branches and makes class separation harder. We denote each setting as num_classes/max_depth. For example, 4/3 means four classes with depth-three branching, while 24/1 means twenty-four classes with minimal internal structure.

These two parameters mainly control between-class crowding and within-class branching. At the same time, like any designed toy, they also affect other properties such as geometry, support overlap, local curvature, and optimization difficulty. We do not fully isolate these secondary effects, and we acknowledge them as part of the limitation of the setup.

The above three configurations illustrate the trade-off. In 4/3, each class forms a deep recursive tree, so the main challenge is to model rich within-class structure while separating only four classes. In 24/1, each class has simple geometry, but the number of classes is much larger, so the main challenge shifts to between-class discrimination. The 12/2 setting lies between these extremes. By sweeping across this space, we can ask when CFG helps, when AG performs better, and when both become inadequate.

The Leaves experiments train a single conditional model over all classes jointly. This means the model shares capacity across classes, and guidance is studied in a more crowded label space rather than in a setting where each class is handled separately.

Ground Truth Unguided CFG AG SGG

4/3: Preserving within-class structure

In the 4/3 T=2^15 regime, the main challenge is to preserve fine within-class structure rather than to separate classes. Because there are only four classes but each class has deep branching, the model must capture detailed conditional geometry. In this setting, unguided sampling gives reasonable class separation but misses some branch detail. CFG tends to over-amplify the class signal and pushes samples toward the main trunk, which reduces structural fidelity. In the AG panel, samples follow the fine branches more closely.

24/1: Separating many classes

In the 24/1 T=2^12 regime, the situation is reversed. Each class has simple internal structure, but there are many classes packed into the same space, so the main difficulty is between-class separation. At the earlier checkpoint, \(T=2^{12}\), unguided sampling often shows class confusion, with samples leaking across nearby class boundaries. CFG is more effective because its stronger conditional contrast sharpens class separation and helps keep samples aligned with the intended class. AG is less helpful in this context, since refinement offers limited benefit when the main problem is not subtle geometry but coarse discrimination among many classes.

Context-dependent behavior

In the examples shown, CFG helps separate nearby classes, while AG preserves more of the branching structure in the four-class example. The intermediate 12/2 case lies between these extremes, and both methods show mixed behavior there. Class count, branching depth, and training duration change together across these examples, so the panels do not isolate the effect of any one factor.

Where the Toy Reaches Its Limits

Leaves makes context dependence visible, but it remains a two-dimensional distribution. Once the question moves beyond coordinate-space behavior to issues such as representation geometry, semantic abstraction, or feature collapse, a toy of this kind can no longer provide a faithful answer.

Beyond coordinates: where 2D toys fail

The comparison below uses three training variants on the Leaves dataset.
